text.p: Amgen Inc Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Gordon Binder said Tuesday the reduced expectations for sales of its key Epogen drug will have a modest impact on 1997 earnings.

While he did not specify the extent of that impact, Amgen said in a 10Q filing Monday it no longer is comfortable with analyst forecasts. The mean analyst estimate is for 1997 earnings of $2.83 per share, according to First Call.
Binder declined to give a new forecast but said he did not disagree with a new estimate by one analyst of $2.67 per share.

However, he said it was difficult to give precise estimates until it becomes clearer how much Epogen sales will drop as a result of changes in Medicare reimbursement policies. The change, which essentially reduces the number of patients who qualify for reimbursement for Epogen use, was announced earlier this year, but the implementation has been delayed twice and it is now due to take effect on September 1.

"We experienced the first wave of reaction and now it appears there is a second wave," Binder said. "I think (doctors) are deciding to reduce Epogen use more than Amgen anticipated. They really don't want to have their claims denied."

Epogen boosts red blood cell count and is commonly used by patients undergoing kidney dialysis who have anemia. Binder said that since the change in reimbursement policies was announced, doctors have taken some patients off the drug entirely. Many of those patients, however, are expected to be put back on it once their hematocrit, or red blood cell, level drops back to a range that again qualifies them for reimbursement.
At the same time, Binder said there are other doctors who have not yet reacted to the policy change but are expected to do so in the third quarter.
Epogen is one of just two products Amgen currently has on the market and last year contributed more than half of Amgen's roughly $2 billion in revenues.
"It is a big product," Binder added. "And patients who need red blood cells will still need this product. It is just a matter of a somewhat lower dose."
Binder said Amgen is "providing guidance to dialysis centers on how to "mazimize patient outcomes to the greatest extent while minimizing the potential of claims being denied."
